title: Koszul polynomial presentations glue over a principal target cover
statement: For an ideal $L$ in a commutative ring $T$, say that $L$ is locally Koszul-regular if for every prime $\mathfrak a\subset T$ containing $L$ there are $u\in T\setminus\mathfrak a$, $r\geq0$, and $a_1,\ldots,a_r\in T_u$ with $LT_u=(a_1,\ldots,a_r)$ and $H_i(K_\bullet(T_u;a_1,\ldots,a_r))=0$ for all $i>0$ [def-weil-ring-localization-away, def-weil-pbc-koszul-regular-sequence]. Let $R\to S$ be a homomorphism of commutative rings for which $S$ is a finitely generated $R$-algebra (there is a surjective $R$-algebra map $R[z_1,\ldots,z_N]\twoheadrightarrow S$ for some finite $N\geq0$) [def-weil-pbc-mv-polynomial-ring]. Let $g_1,\ldots,g_t\in S$ generate the unit ideal, where $t\geq0$. Suppose that for each $j$ there are $n_j\geq0$ and a surjective $R$-algebra map $\alpha_j:R[x_1,\ldots,x_{n_j}]\twoheadrightarrow S_{g_j}$ whose kernel is locally Koszul-regular. Then there are $n\geq0$ and a surjective $R$-algebra map $\alpha:R[x_1,\ldots,x_n]\twoheadrightarrow S$ whose kernel is locally Koszul-regular. No flatness or Noetherian hypothesis is imposed; an empty cover is allowed and forces $S=0$.

proof.text: Choose the finite polynomial surjection $\alpha:P=R[x_1,\ldots,x_n]\twoheadrightarrow S$ supplied by finite generation and put $I=\ker\alpha$. For each $j$ lift $g_j$ to $h_j\in P$. We will prove that this fixed $I$ is locally Koszul-regular; it is unnecessary to glue the different sets of polynomial variables.

For each $j$ let $\beta_j:P[z]\to S_{g_j}$ send $z$ to $g_j^{-1}$ and restrict on $P$ to $\alpha$ followed by localization. By [lem-weil-pbc-localization-away-polynomial-quotient], $S[z]\to S_{g_j}$ is surjective with kernel $(g_jz-1)$. The coefficient map $P[z]\to S[z]$ is surjective with kernel $IP[z]$: a polynomial maps to zero exactly when each coefficient belongs to $I$. Consequently $\beta_j$ is surjective and has kernel $J_j=IP[z]+(h_jz-1)$. Indeed, a multiple of $g_jz-1$ lifts to a multiple of $h_jz-1$, and its difference from the original polynomial has all coefficients in $I$. Regard $P[z]$ as the polynomial ring over $R$ in $n+1$ variables.

Apply [lem-sfb-koszul-polynomial-presentation-independence] to the given $\alpha_j:R[x_1,\ldots,x_{n_j}]\twoheadrightarrow S_{g_j}$ and the presentation $\beta_j$ of Step 2. Its hypothesis on the first kernel is precisely the hypothesis of the item. It follows that $J_j$ is locally Koszul-regular. This application imposes neither flatness nor a Noetherian assumption.

Fix a prime $\mathfrak q\subset P$ containing $I$. Some $h_j$ lies outside $\mathfrak q$: otherwise a relation $1=\sum_j s_jg_j$ in $S$, lifted coefficient by coefficient to $P$, would imply $1\in\mathfrak q$. For this $j$, the ideal $\mathfrak q'=\mathfrak q P[z]+(h_jz-1)$ is prime, since its quotient is the nonzero domain $(P/\mathfrak q)[1/\overline h_j]$; the inverse-variable quotient is given by [lem-weil-pbc-localization-away-polynomial-quotient]. It contains $J_j$. Unpack Step 3 at this prime to obtain $v\notin\mathfrak q'$ and finite Koszul-regular generators for $(J_j)_v$. Apply [lem-sfb-koszul-inverse-equation-elimination] with $A=P$, $h=h_j$, and this witness. It yields $d\notin\mathfrak q$ and finite Koszul-regular generators for $IP_d$, exactly the required neighbourhood.

Step 4 supplies the witnesses at every prime containing $I$, so $I$ is locally Koszul-regular and $\alpha$ proves the conclusion. If the cover is empty, its unit-ideal hypothesis says $1=0$ in $S$. Then $S=0$, $I=P$, and there are no prime ideals containing $I$; the same condition is vacuous. Zero-variable presentations and empty sequences remain allowed throughout.
